title: Fine-Tuning Strategies: Full vs PEFT
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Fine-Tuning Strategies: Full vs PEFT ##### The model that forgot Hindi A team in Gurugram full fine-tuned Llama-3-8B on 40,000 English customer-support conversations. Learning rate 2e-5, three epochs, standard recipe. On their support task it was excellent — a 14-point improvement over the base model. Then someone tested it in Hindi, which the base model handled reasonably well. It produced English. Asked directly in Devanagari, it replied in English. Asked to translate, it refused and answered the perceived support question instead. Multilingual benchmark scores had dropped from 61% to 23%. **Catastrophic forgetting.** Three epochs of gradient updates on English-only data at full learning rate had overwritten the multilingual capability that pretraining spent trillions of tokens building. They redid it with LoRA at rank 16. Support-task improvement: 13 points — one point worse. Hindi capability: **unchanged at 61%**. That comparison is the practical heart of the full-versus-PEFT decision, and it is more nuanced than "PEFT is cheaper." PEFT is also **safer**, because a frozen base model cannot be overwritten. ##### The strategy landscape ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Need to adapt
a base model"] --> B{"Dataset size?"} B -->|"< 500 examples"| C["Few-shot prompting
or RAG"] B -->|"500 - 50k"| D{"Preserve general
capability?"} B -->|"> 50k, new domain"| E{"Budget?"} D -->|Yes| F["LoRA / QLoRA
r=8-32"] D -->|"No, narrow task"| G{"Memory available?"} G -->|Ample| H["Full FT, low LR,
1-2 epochs"] G -->|Limited| F E -->|High| I["Full FT or
continued pretraining"] E -->|Limited| J["LoRA r=64-128
on all modules"] ``` | Method | Trainable | Memory (7B) | Forgetting | Quality ceiling | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Full FT** | 100% | ~88 GB | **High** | Highest | | **LoRA** | 0.1–1% | ~18 GB | Very low | ~98% of full | | **QLoRA** | 0.1–1% | **~6 GB** | Very low | ~97% of full | | **DoRA** | 0.1–1% | ~19 GB | Very low | ~99% of full | | **Adapters** | 1–5% | ~22 GB | Low | ~97% of full | | **Prefix tuning** | ~0.1% | ~16 GB | None | ~90% of full | | **Prompt tuning** | <0.1% | ~15 GB | None | ~85%, scale-dependent | | **BitFit** | ~0.08% | ~15 GB | Low | ~90% | ##### Full fine-tuning Every parameter updated. The highest ceiling and the highest risk. ```python from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, TrainingArguments, Trainer model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="flash_attention_2", ) model.gradient_checkpointing_enable() args = TrainingArguments( output_dir="./full-ft", learning_rate=1e-5, # ← LOW. Lower than you think. num_train_epochs=2, # ← 1-2, not 3+ per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=16, warmup_ratio=0.03, lr_scheduler_type="cosine", weight_decay=0.0, # often 0 for short fine-tunes max_grad_norm=1.0, bf16=True, gradient_checkpointing=True, optim="adamw_torch_fused", eval_strategy="steps", eval_steps=100, save_strategy="steps", save_steps=100, load_best_model_at_end=True, seed=42, ) ``` **When full fine-tuning is genuinely the right call:** - **Continued pretraining** on a new domain or language with 100M+ tokens. - **A fundamentally different task** the base model cannot do at all. - **You do not need general capability** — a narrow classifier, for example. - **You have the budget** and want the last 1–2 points. **Memory:** roughly 88 GB for a 7B model in bf16 with Adam, from Day 1's arithmetic. Needs FSDP or ZeRO-3 across multiple GPUs, or CPU offloading. **The learning rate is the safety dial.** 1e-5 to 2e-5 for instruction tuning; 5e-6 or lower if you are worried about forgetting. The Gurugram team used 2e-5 for three epochs, which is aggressive. ##### Catastrophic forgetting The mechanism is straightforward: gradient descent moves weights toward the new task's optimum, and nothing in the objective preserves the old capabilities. Weights encoding Hindi grammar get overwritten because nothing in the English support data needs them. **Measure it, always.** This is the step teams skip: ```python def forgetting_report(base_model, tuned_model, benchmarks, tokenizer): """benchmarks: {name: eval_fn(model, tokenizer) -> score}""" rows = [] for name, fn in benchmarks.items(): b = fn(base_model, tokenizer) t = fn(tuned_model, tokenizer) rows.append({ "benchmark": name, "base": round(b, 3), "tuned": round(t, 3), "delta": round(t - b, 3), "retention_pct": round(100 * t / b, 1) if b else None, }) return rows # Always include capabilities you did NOT fine-tune on BENCHMARKS = { "target_task": eval_support_quality, "mmlu": eval_mmlu, "hindi_qa": eval_hindi, # ← the one that caught it "gsm8k": eval_math, "instruction_following": eval_ifeval, } ``` **Mitigations, in order of practicality:** 1. **Use PEFT.** A frozen base cannot be overwritten. This is the strongest and simplest defence. 2. **Lower the learning rate.** 5e-6 rather than 2e-5. 3. **Fewer epochs.** One or two, not five. 4. **Replay data.** Mix 5–20% general instruction data into your task-specific set. 5. **Freeze early layers.** They hold the most general features. 6. **KL regularisation** toward the base model's outputs. ```python def build_replay_mixture(task_data, general_data, replay_frac=0.10, seed=42): """Mix general instruction data into a task-specific set.""" import random rng = random.Random(seed) n_replay = int(len(task_data) * replay_frac / (1 - replay_frac)) sampled = rng.sample(general_data, min(n_replay, len(general_data))) mixed = task_data + sampled rng.shuffle(mixed) return mixed ``` Ten percent replay from a general instruction set typically recovers most of the lost capability at negligible cost — and it is two lines. ##### PEFT: the shared idea All PEFT methods freeze the base model and train a small number of new parameters. They differ in *where* those parameters sit. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph BLOCK["Transformer block — frozen base"] A["input"] --> B["Attention W_q W_k W_v W_o"] B --> C["MLP W_up W_down"] C --> D["output"] end E["LoRA: low-rank ΔW
added in parallel
to frozen matrices"] -.-> B E -.-> C F["Adapter: small bottleneck
inserted in series"] -.-> C G["Prefix: trainable vectors
prepended to K,V"] -.-> B H["Prompt: trainable
embeddings at input"] -.-> A I["BitFit: train only
bias terms"] -.-> B ``` **LoRA** — Day 12 covers this in depth. Parallel low-rank matrices, mergeable at inference, currently the default. **Adapters** (Houlsby et al., 2019) — the original. Small bottleneck MLPs inserted *in series* after attention and feedforward: ```python class Adapter(nn.Module): def __init__(self, d_model, bottleneck=64): super().__init__() self.down = nn.Linear(d_model, bottleneck) self.up = nn.Linear(bottleneck, d_model) nn.init.zeros_(self.up.weight) # start as identity nn.init.zeros_(self.up.bias) def forward(self, x): return x + self.up(F.gelu(self.down(x))) ``` Their weakness is **inference latency**. Because they sit in series they cannot be merged into the base weights, adding roughly 5–10% to every forward pass. This is precisely why LoRA displaced them. **Prefix tuning** (Li & Liang, 2021) prepends trainable key and value vectors to every attention layer: ```python class PrefixTuning(nn.Module): def __init__(self, n_layers, n_heads, head_dim, prefix_len=20): super().__init__() self.prefix_k = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n_layers, n_heads, prefix_len, head_dim) * 0.02) self.prefix_v = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(n_layers, n_heads, prefix_len, head_dim) * 0.02) ``` Very few parameters and zero forgetting, since nothing in the base model changes. But it **consumes context length** — a 20-token prefix costs 20 tokens of your window at every layer — and it is fiddly to train stably. **Prompt tuning** (Lester et al., 2021) is the simplest: trainable embeddings prepended at the input only. It works surprisingly well *at scale* — at 10B+ parameters it approaches full fine-tuning — and poorly below about 1B. **BitFit** trains only bias terms. About 0.08% of parameters, competitive on classification, weak on generation. A useful baseline. ##### Choosing: the decision framework Your assignment asks for this, so here is a defensible version. ```python from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class TuningContext: n_examples: int gpu_memory_gb: float base_model_B: float preserve_general: bool n_tasks_to_serve: int latency_critical: bool domain_shift: str # "none" | "moderate" | "large" def recommend_strategy(ctx: TuningContext) -> dict: reasons = [] if ctx.n_examples < 500: return {"method": "few-shot prompting or RAG", "reason": "too few examples; fine-tuning will overfit"} full_ft_memory = ctx.base_model_B * 18 # ~18 GB per B with Adam bf16 can_full_ft = ctx.gpu_memory_gb >= full_ft_memory if ctx.domain_shift == "large" and ctx.n_examples > 100_000 and can_full_ft: return {"method": "full fine-tuning / continued pretraining", "lr": 1e-5, "epochs": 2, "reason": "large domain shift with enough data to justify it", "caution": "measure forgetting; add 10% replay data"} if ctx.n_tasks_to_serve > 1: reasons.append("multiple tasks → unmerged LoRA adapters, hot-swappable") if ctx.preserve_general: reasons.append("must preserve general capability → frozen base") if not can_full_ft: reasons.append(f"needs {full_ft_memory:.0f}GB for full FT, have {ctx.gpu_memory_gb:.0f}GB") rank = 16 if ctx.n_examples < 10_000 else 32 if ctx.n_examples < 100_000 else 64 method = "QLoRA" if ctx.gpu_memory_gb < ctx.base_model_B * 3 else "LoRA" return { "method": method, "rank": rank, "alpha": rank * 2, "lr": 2e-4, "epochs": 3 if ctx.n_examples < 10_000 else 2, "target_modules": ["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"], "merge_at_inference": ctx.latency_critical and ctx.n_tasks_to_serve == 1, "reasons": reasons, } print(recommend_strategy(TuningContext( n_examples=40_000, gpu_memory_gb=80, base_model_B=8, preserve_general=True, n_tasks_to_serve=3, latency_critical=False, domain_shift="moderate"))) ``` ##### Continual learning Adapting repeatedly over time — a support model updated quarterly, say — compounds the forgetting problem. **Practical strategies:** - **Adapter accumulation.** Keep one LoRA per version; serve the latest, retain the ability to roll back. Storage is tens of megabytes each. - **Replay buffers.** Retain a sample from every previous task and mix it into each new training run. - **Elastic Weight Consolidation** penalises changes to parameters that were important for previous tasks, weighted by Fisher information. Principled, and rarely used in LLM practice because computing the Fisher matrix at scale is expensive. - **Model merging** — combine independently fine-tuned models by averaging weights (Model Soups), or by task arithmetic where task vectors `θ_tuned − θ_base` are added and subtracted. ```python def merge_task_vectors(base_sd, tuned_sds, weights=None): """Task arithmetic: θ_merged = θ_base + Σ wᵢ(θᵢ − θ_base).""" weights = weights or [1.0 / len(tuned_sds)] * len(tuned_sds) merged = {k: v.clone() for k, v in base_sd.items()} for sd, w in zip(tuned_sds, weights): for k in merged: if k in sd and merged[k].is_floating_point(): merged[k] += w * (sd[k] - base_sd[k]) return merged ``` Task arithmetic is surprisingly effective and cheap. Merging LoRA adapters trained on different tasks often produces a model competent at both, which is a much better outcome than sequential fine-tuning. ##### Building the quality-cost frontier The mini project asks for a benchmark. Structure it as a frontier, not a single winner: ```python import time import torch def benchmark_method(name, train_fn, eval_fns, base_model_fn): torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats() t0 = time.perf_counter() model, n_trainable = train_fn() train_time = time.perf_counter() - t0 peak_gb = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9 scores = {k: fn(model) for k, fn in eval_fns.items()} return { "method": name, "trainable_params": n_trainable, "trainable_pct": round(100 * n_trainable / 8e9, 3), "peak_memory_gb": round(peak_gb, 1), "train_minutes": round(train_time / 60, 1), **{f"score_{k}": round(v, 3) for k, v in scores.items()}, } ``` Report target-task score **and** retention on unrelated benchmarks. A method that wins on the target task and loses 30 points of general capability is not the winner — it is a different trade. ##### Common mistakes - **Full fine-tuning without measuring forgetting** — the Hindi disaster. - **Full FT learning rate above 2e-5.** - **Three or more epochs** on a small dataset. - **No replay data** when general capability matters. - **PEFT learning rate set like full FT.** LoRA wants 1e-4 to 3e-4, roughly 10× higher. - **LoRA on only `q_proj` and `v_proj`** because the original paper did. - **Adapters when latency matters** — they cannot be merged. - **Prompt tuning on a sub-1B model**, where it barely works. - **Merging adapters** when you need to serve multiple tasks from one base. - **Evaluating only on the target task**, missing the regression everywhere else. - **Assuming PEFT always underperforms.** At typical dataset sizes it is within 1–2 points, and it wins on retention. ##### Hands-on: run both and compare Your practical task fine-tunes the same base model with full FT and LoRA on one task, comparing quality, memory, and forgetting. Use a small model — 1B or under — so full FT is feasible. **Include at least one held-out capability you did not train on**, ideally in a different language. That column is the whole point; without it you will conclude full FT is simply better. The mini project benchmarks three PEFT methods and reports a quality-cost frontier. LoRA, prefix tuning, and BitFit make a good trio because they represent genuinely different mechanisms. Plot target-task score against trainable parameters on log axes and mark the Pareto frontier. Add a second panel showing retention on a general benchmark — that second panel is where the interesting story usually is. The assignment is a decision framework given dataset size, budget, and deployment needs. Extend the `recommend_strategy` function, then validate it against five real scenarios and check whether its recommendation matches what you would advise. Where it disagrees with your judgement, either the function is missing a factor or your intuition is wrong — resolving that is the exercise. ##### Key takeaways - **Full fine-tuning has the highest ceiling and the highest risk** — three epochs at 2e-5 on English data erased multilingual capability the base model spent trillions of tokens acquiring. - **PEFT is safer, not just cheaper.** A frozen base model cannot be overwritten, which is why LoRA lost one point on the target task and zero points everywhere else. - **Always evaluate capabilities you did not fine-tune on.** Forgetting is invisible if you only measure the target metric. - **LoRA displaced adapters because it merges**; prefix and prompt tuning cost context length and only work well at scale. - **Mix 10% general replay data** into any full fine-tune, keep the learning rate at or below 2e-5, and cap epochs at two — three cheap defences against the most expensive mistake in this article.
